newsitem.title: FRANCE: French budget went as far as possible - Arthuis.
newsitem.headline: French budget went as far as possible - Arthuis.

text.p: France's 1997 budget will go as far as possible in reducing France's public deficit without damaging the economy and social unity, French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Tuesday.
Speaking in a parliamentary debate two days before a 24-hour public sector strike, he also said the budget was not recessive since it aimed to encourage consumption through income tax cuts.
"I think we have gone as far as it was possible to go without losing sight of economic development and social unity," he said.

The budget would help France meet its objective of reducing the public deficit to below three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 from a forecast four percent this year and five percent last year to prepare for European monetary union.

"For this year, we promised to remain below four percent of GDP. I am very confident this objective will be respected, despite a slower than expected recovery in welfare accounts," he said. "In 1997, we want to get below the three percent level."
Civil servants, teachers, rail and power workers will strike on Thursday to protest the government's austerity drive and planned cuts in the civil service contained in the 1997 budget.
Airlines have also been asked to cut back to a minimum service due to a strike by air traffic controllers and some ground staff.
The strike will be the first real test to show if the will is there for the kind of showdown which crippled France at the end of last year.
Unions say the drive to cut public spending is hurting the economy and partly responsible for an unemployment rate which has reached a record 12.6 percent.

Arthuis however argued that the government would cut income taxes next year, while it would also release a further 15 billion francs into the economy by allowing people to withdraw money early from popular savings plans (PEPs).

"Some people would have you believe that the budget may be recessive. No...it releases new margins in favour of consumer spending with the reduction in income taxes and the liquidation of premiums on PEPs," he said.

The government is scrapping some tax breaks to help finance its reduction in income taxes -- prompting a one-day strike by French journalists on Tuesday protesting abolition of a tax allowance which they say is part of their pay.
Arthuis also said that fighting unemployment remained a government priority, and said it would make new reductions in payroll charges as soon as economic growth allows.

"As soon as our determined and coherent policy in favour of growth returns enough room for manoeuvre, we will begin a resolute drive to make new reductions in payroll charges because these are what weigh on our competitiveness and our employment," he told parliament.
